problem_text:
A logistics company must devise a procurement and storage strategy for a critical fuel additive over an operational window spanning 18 weeks.  
The starting stockpile at the outset of the planning interval is 18 thousand liters.  
In each week \( t = 1, \dots, 18 \), the vendor permits the company to submit a fuel‑additive purchase, the volume of which must fall between 16 and 28 thousand liters.  
Any order placed is delivered instantly, becoming available immediately to meet weekly requirements or to replenish reserves.  
Weekly consumption of the additive is forecasted as follows:  

* Week 1: 28 thousand liters  
* Week 2: 27 thousand liters  
* Week 3: 26 thousand liters  
* Week 4: 23 thousand liters  
* Week 5: 35 thousand liters  
* Week 6: 53 thousand liters  
* Week 7: 10 thousand liters  
* Week 8: 50 thousand liters  
* Week 9: 13 thousand liters  
* Week 10: 43 thousand liters  
* Week 11: 59 thousand liters  
* Week 12: 59 thousand liters  
* Week 13: 14 thousand liters  
* Week 14: 10 thousand liters  
* Week 15: 50 thousand liters  
* Week 16: 28 thousand liters  
* Week 17: 19 thousand liters  
* Week 18: 59 thousand liters  

Stock‑outs are tolerated; any unsatisfied weekly demand is simply lost and will not be fulfilled later.  
Throughout the 18‑week horizon, additive volumes may be treated as continuous quantities, and the total on‑site inventory at any moment must not surpass the storage‑tank capacity of 49 thousand liters.  
The aggregate expense comprises three elements: the procurement cost, amounting to 3 per thousand liters purchased; the storage cost, equal to 1 per thousand liters held over from one week to the next; and the shortage penalty, set at 11 per thousand liters of unmet weekly demand.  
The objective is to identify the optimal purchase quantity each week and to monitor the ensuing stockpile and shortage levels, thereby minimizing total expenditure.
